question.text: Per NISM Ch 2.3.6 and 2.6.1, which statement about Fund of Funds (FoF) structures in the AIF context is MOST accurate?

answer.text: FoFs are AIFs that do not invest directly in investee companies but invest in other AIFs; they offer risk diversification by accessing multiple thematic funds but carry two layers of management fees, which materially erodes investor net return.
FoFs are prohibited in India under the AIF Regulations 2012.
FoFs can only invest in listed equity ETFs, not in AIFs.
FoFs pay zero total fees because SEBI caps the combined fee layer at 0%.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Series XIX-C p.38 (Ch 2.3.6), FoFs are AIFs that do not invest directly in investee companies; they invest in other AIFs and provide risk diversification by accessing several thematic funds. Per p.45 (Ch 2.6.1), because the FoF manager invests in multiple underlying funds, fees are substantially higher than single-strategy hedge funds due to fees charged by each underlying fund plus an additional layer of management fees at the FoF level. The Trap: Option B is incorrect — FoFs are a recognised AIF sub-type. Option C contradicts the source definition (FoFs invest in other AIFs, not only listed ETFs). Option D is wrong because SEBI does not cap combined fees at 0%. Note: Ground the FoF answer strictly in the structure, diversification benefit, and two-layer fee point set out on p.38 and p.45.
